card: CivicOps Mumbai + WardProof|Every complaint has an owner. Every rupee has a reason.
text: This is CivicOps Mumbai, with WardProof. In one line: every complaint has an owner, and every rupee has a reason. We built it at the Claude Impact Lab in Mumbai, on the organisers' synthetic data. In the next six minutes, I will walk you through every screen, the way a resident, a ward officer, a reviewer, and any member of the public would use it.

This is the home page. It has three doors: report a problem, see where the money went, and watch the city live. The numbers are real totals from the dataset: about thirteen crore rupees billed on road repairs in the monsoon budget period, and about three and a half crore where a bill needs an explanation. Every number opens the records behind it.

The live dashboard is the city at a glance, made for a big screen. The map is a real map of Mumbai, with all twenty four wards. Colours show how much of each ward's budget is used, or how many problems are open. Red dots are urgent complaints. On the right, a live feed shows every action as it happens, and the counters refresh every ten seconds.

The Ward Explorer lets anyone pick a ward, on the map or from the list. Here is K West, which covers Andheri West, Juhu and Vile Parle West. You can see its budget used, the money questioned, open complaints, and flood spots. Extra layers show flood hotspots, and roads that keep breaking.

Now our newest idea: a QR code for every road. Every road repair comes with a free repair guarantee, called the defect liability period. Concrete roads get ten years, and asphalt gets three. If the road breaks inside that period, the contractor must fix it for free. But nobody knows when that guarantee ends. The road directory shows every road, with its guarantee counting down.

This is what you see when you scan the QR on a road. The big clock says how long free repairs remain, and who must do them. Below it, a question in red: paid twice? The city paid for repairs while the guarantee was still running. Every bill is listed, with a link to its details. And there is one big button: report a problem on this exact road.
This is the printable site board. Fix it on the road, and anyone with a phone can scan it. The QR leads straight to the road page you just saw.

On a phone, it looks like this. The guarantee comes first, then the money, then the report button, always within reach of your thumb. You can also scan a road from inside the app, with the Scan QR button at the bottom of the screen.

Next, public spending: where did the money go? For each ward, we follow the money from the approved budget, to the work order, to the bill, the evidence, and the review. The bars show the budget against what was billed. Four wards billed more than their budget. Questioned money is counted once per work order, so nothing is counted twice.

Here is one example from the dataset: a repair on Link Road in Juhu. The bill was twenty three thousand, three hundred and eleven rupees. The city's own rate card says it should cost about twelve thousand, two hundred. That is ninety percent more. The road also broke again within thirty days. We never call this fraud. We ask a question, in public, with a deadline.

The accountability view checks every bill fairly. A contractor is only compared with what is normal for the repair method they used, and delays on heavy rain days are taken out. Normal variation is never flagged. It also suggests where the next rupee should go, preferring repairs that last.
Now, the people who do the work. Each role signs in separately: the resident, the ward officer, the ward office, the auditor, and the super admin. On the demo site, one click signs you in.
A resident sees each of their reports with a simple progress ring, the current step, and the deadline. When a repair is verified, the report turns green, at one hundred percent.

To report a problem, the resident picks a category, answers two or three simple questions, and drops a pin on the real map, or uses GPS. Before submitting, they already see which ward and which team will get it, and how urgent it is. This report came from a road QR, so the road is already filled in.
The ward officer sees their queue, with overdue, due soon, and unassigned work first. Each card says what to do next.

Opening a ticket shows everything on one screen: who owns it, who is doing the work, including the contractor, the next step, and the deadline. The progress trail shows each step, with the time it happened. The officer records the first action, uploads photo proof, and sends it for review.

The super admin runs the command centre: new reports as they arrive, escalations when deadlines are missed, and every ward's performance at a glance. When an officer is assigned, they get an alert straight away.
When the work is finished, the reviewer compares the before and after photos with a slider. Claude can describe what changed, but a person always makes the decision, and records the reason.

The auditor sees every question about spending: the amount, the reason, which office must answer, and by when. If an office does not respond in time, the case is escalated automatically, and the public can see it.
Everything also works in Marathi and in Hindi. Switch the language, and the whole page changes, not just the menu.

So that is CivicOps Mumbai, with WardProof. Complaints reach the right ward with a visible deadline. Repairs are proven with photos, and checked by a person. Every rupee can be traced and questioned in public. And every road carries its own QR. Thank you.
